scenes.title: Renewable Energy Resources
scenes.text: Hello and welcome back to JD Science. In today's lesson we will examine renewable energy resources, including solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal and biomass. We will consider how they work, their advantages and their limitations, and finish with a GCSE examination question. Subscribe to JD Science and visit jdscience.co.uk for further revision.

scenes.title: Renewable resources
scenes.text: Renewable energy resources are replenished naturally on human timescales. They can reduce dependence on finite fuels, although they still have environmental impacts and may need supporting infrastructure. When comparing renewable resources, explain how energy is transferred, what makes the resource useful and what limits its use.

scenes.title: Solar and wind
scenes.text: Solar photovoltaic panels convert energy transferred by sunlight into electrical energy. They produce electricity without burning fuel during operation, but output depends on daylight, weather, location and season. Solar thermal systems are different: they use sunlight to heat water. Wind turbines use the kinetic energy of moving air to turn blades connected to a generator. They have low direct emissions during operation, but output varies with wind conditions and installations can affect landscapes and wildlife.

scenes.title: Hydroelectric and tidal
scenes.text: Hydroelectric stations use water stored at height. As the water flows downhill, its gravitational potential energy store decreases and energy is transferred to the kinetic energy stores of the moving water and turbine, then electrically through a generator. Hydroelectric generation can be controllable where reservoirs are available, but dams may be costly and may flood habitats or settlements. Tidal systems exploit the predictable movement of seawater caused by tides. Tidal barrages and tidal-stream turbines can generate electricity, but suitable locations are limited and marine ecosystems may be affected.

scenes.title: Biomass
scenes.text: Biomass consists of organic material such as wood, agricultural residues or specially grown crops. It can be burnt to provide heat or electricity, or processed into biofuels. Biomass can be renewable when harvested and replenished responsibly, but it is not automatically carbon-neutral or sustainable. Growing, harvesting, transporting and burning biomass can cause greenhouse gas emissions, land-use change and competition with food production.

scenes.title: Hydroelectric transfer
scenes.text: Let us work through a hydroelectric energy-transfer example. Water in a high reservoir has a gravitational potential energy store. As it descends, this store decreases and the kinetic energy of the flowing water increases. The moving water does mechanical work on a turbine, and the generator transfers energy electrically to the grid. Some energy is dissipated to the surroundings because of friction and other losses.

scenes.title: Your turn
scenes.text: Now it is your turn. Describe how a solar photovoltaic panel generates electricity. Pause the video.

scenes.title: Worked answer
scenes.text: Energy from sunlight reaches the cells by electromagnetic radiation. The photovoltaic cells convert part of that incoming energy into electrical energy. A high-quality answer distinguishes the radiation transfer from the electrical output.

scenes.title: GCSE-style question
scenes.text: Here is a three-mark GCSE-style question. Explain why biomass can be renewable but may still contribute to climate change. Model answer: biomass can be replenished by growing replacement plants. Burning it releases carbon dioxide, and its overall climate impact also depends on cultivation, transport, land-use change and how quickly plants regrow. Award one mark for replenishment, one for emissions and one for a relevant life-cycle or land-use consideration.

scenes.title: Keep practising
scenes.text: Remember that renewable does not necessarily mean impact-free. Use balanced scientific comparisons in your GCSE answers. Subscribe to JD Science and visit jdscience.co.uk. Thank you for watching.
